questions.q: A stock has a very narrow bid-ask spread but only 50 shares resting at the best price on each side. Which dimension of liquidity is weak despite the tight spread?
options: Tightness
Depth
Resiliency
Tick size
questions.explain: Tightness (spread width) can be favorable while depth (size available near the best price) is thin — liquidity requires all three dimensions, not just a narrow spread.

options: A regulatory fee charged on large trades
The price movement caused by a trader's own large order consuming resting liquidity at successive price levels
The difference between a stock's opening and closing price
The commission a broker charges on an order
questions.explain: Market impact is the price movement an order itself causes once it exhausts resting size at the best price and has to fill at progressively worse prices.

questions.q: What distinguishes the "permanent" component of market impact from the "temporary" component?
options: Permanent impact only affects bonds, not equities
Temporary impact partly reverses as the book refills; permanent impact sticks because the large order conveys information
Permanent impact is always larger in dollar terms
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: Temporary impact fades as the book refills after the order finishes. Permanent impact persists because a large order signals information that shifts the market's view of fair value.

questions.q: How does a VWAP execution algorithm differ from a TWAP algorithm?
options: VWAP trades equal-sized pieces at equal time intervals; TWAP sizes pieces to match typical volume
TWAP trades equal-sized pieces at equal time intervals; VWAP sizes pieces to match the market's typical volume by time of day
VWAP can only be used for bonds; TWAP can only be used for equities
They are two names for the exact same algorithm
questions.explain: TWAP splits an order into equal pieces at regular time intervals regardless of volume. VWAP instead sizes each piece in proportion to the market's typical trading volume at that time of day.

questions.q: Why would an institutional trader use VWAP or TWAP instead of simply submitting one large market order?
options: To guarantee the absolute lowest possible commission
To reduce market impact and slippage by spreading execution out instead of walking through the order book all at once
Because exchanges prohibit single large market orders entirely
Because VWAP and TWAP orders settle faster than market orders
questions.explain: Splitting a large order over time reduces how much it depletes resting liquidity at any one moment, keeping the average execution price closer to the market's natural price and reducing slippage.
